author: "NEISS 2019-2024"
format:
  dashboard:
    theme: cosmo
    embed-resources: true
---

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

# trampoline.rds is made by prep.R: it keeps the trampoline cases
# (product code 1233) from the NEISS files 2019-2024 and adds labels.
tramp <- read_rds("trampoline.rds") |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group,
                            levels = c("0-2", "3-5", "6-11", "12-17", "18-34", "35+")))

# IMPORTANT: a national estimate is the SUM OF WEIGHTS, not the number of rows.
```

# Overview

## Row {height="25%"}

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "ER visits per year (estimate)"
list(icon = "hospital", color = "primary",
     value = format(round(sum(tramp$weight) / 6), big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Patients younger than 12"
pct_kids <- 100 * sum(tramp$weight[tramp$age < 12]) / sum(tramp$weight)
list(icon = "people", color = "warning", value = paste0(round(pct_kids), "%"))
```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Diagnosed with a fracture"
pct_frac <- 100 * sum(tramp$weight[tramp$diagnosis == "Fracture"]) / sum(tramp$weight)
list(icon = "bandaid", color = "danger", value = paste0(round(pct_frac), "%"))
```

## Row

### Column {width="35%"}

::: card
**Product:** trampolines (NEISS product code 1233), 2019 to 2024.

**Questions**

1.  Which ages are hurt the most, and how badly?
2.  How do the injuries happen at home compared with trampoline parks?
3.  Did the pandemic change where children got hurt?
:::

### Column {width="65%"}

```{r}
#| title: "In 2020, trampoline-park injuries fell by half while home injuries rose"
by_year <- tramp |>
  filter(place != "Other/not recorded") |>
  group_by(year, place) |>
  summarise(estimate = sum(weight), .groups = "drop")

p <- ggplot(by_year, aes(year, estimate, color = place)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Home" = "#2a6fdb",
                                "Trampoline park/rec place" = "#e07b1f")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "ER visits (national estimate)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplotly(p)
```

# Who is hurt

## Column

```{r}
#| title: "Most patients are young children; the most common age is 6"
by_age <- tramp |>
  mutate(age_year = floor(age)) |>
  filter(age_year <= 40) |>
  group_by(age_year) |>
  summarise(per_year = sum(weight) / 6)

p <- ggplot(by_age, aes(age_year, per_year)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6fdb") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "ER visits per year (estimate)") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplotly(p)
```

## Column

```{r}
#| title: "Children 3 to 5 have the highest share of fractures"
frac_age <- tramp |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(percent = 100 * sum(weight * (diagnosis == "Fracture")) / sum(weight))

p <- ggplot(frac_age, aes(age_group, percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#d64545") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "% of injuries that are fractures") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplotly(p)
```

# How it happens

## Column

```{r}
#| title: "Home: other jumpers and falls off the trampoline. Parks: bad landings"
# The injury type is read from the narrative in prep.R. Narratives that do not
# say how the injury happened are left out of this plot.
mech_place <- tramp |>
  filter(place != "Other/not recorded",
         !mechanism %in% c("Not described", "Fell (no detail)")) |>
  group_by(place, mechanism) |>
  summarise(estimate = sum(weight), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(place) |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * estimate / sum(estimate))

p <- ggplot(mech_place, aes(reorder(mechanism, percent), percent, fill = place)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Home" = "#2a6fdb",
                               "Trampoline park/rec place" = "#e07b1f")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of injuries at that place", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplotly(p)
```

## Column

```{r}
#| title: "Falling off the trampoline is the most likely to break a bone"
frac_mech <- tramp |>
  filter(mechanism != "Not described") |>
  group_by(mechanism) |>
  summarise(percent = 100 * sum(weight * (diagnosis == "Fracture")) / sum(weight))

p <- ggplot(frac_mech, aes(reorder(mechanism, percent), percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#d64545") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of injuries that are fractures") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplotly(p)
```

# Narratives

```{r}
#| title: "ER narratives, 2024 (search for words such as NET, FLIP, PARK)"
tramp |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  transmute(Date = date, Age = round(age, 1), Sex = sex, Place = place,
            Diagnosis = diagnosis, Narrative = narrative) |>
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 10))
```

# Findings

::: card
### What we learned

**1. Young children are hurt the most, and badly.** About 117,000 people go to an ER each year after a trampoline injury, and about 70% of them are under 12. Children 3 to 5 have the highest share of fractures (about 42%), so small children do not just "bounce back."

**2. At home, the danger is other jumpers and the edge.** On home trampolines, about 29% of the described injuries involve more than one jumper and 31% are falls off the trampoline, compared with 17% and 13% at trampoline parks. At parks, more than half are bad landings. Falls off the trampoline are the most likely to end in a fracture (43%). Advice for parents: one jumper at a time, and use a net.

**3. Surprise: the pandemic moved injuries to backyards.** In 2020, when trampoline parks closed, park injuries fell by about half (from about 41,000 to 22,000), while home injuries rose to their highest level (about 45,000).

**Limits.** NEISS counts injuries, not jumpers, so we cannot say that home trampolines are riskier per jump. About 45% of cases have no location, and the injury type is read from the narratives with simple rules, so those numbers are approximate.
:::
